additionalInformation: Tuesday 3/10/26 at approx 1:30 am I received an alarm via SCADA/Win911 for effluent filter.  I responded and arrived at the WWTP at approx 1:45am.  I found our effluent sand filters to be overwhelmed with effluent and solids from our clarifiers.  I shut down the air to the aeration tanks to settle out the solids,  then shut down backwash pumps for sand filters, closed one side of our contact tanks and opened the other which was empty at the time for cleaning to trap solid overflow, and then opened bypass valve approx 1/4 open to get flow levels under control.  Wasting was increased.  High flows most likely due to .83 of rain Friday 3/6 and high temps melting 3+ feet of snow.  Solids where contained to contact tank.  Air was restored to aeration process by 6am 3/10.  Additional wasting continued to restore sludge blanket levels in clarifiers.  Bypass remained approx 1/4 open 3/10, 3/11 started closing slowly 3/12 and closed completely 3/13 at 10:20am.  Public notifications where made Wednesday 3/11 in the morning,  along with trying to gain access to Sewage overflow system through Ma Dep.

eventType: SSO – System Surcharging Under High Flow Conditions
additionalInformation:
The Distribution Box (D-box) on the west side of the plant grounds had some spillage of sewage that flows into the aeration tanks.  The plant had high inflows, 3-3.5 MGD, upon Saturday 21st from rain and two influent pumps were used to handle the inflows- a 50hp lead pump and a 20 hp lag pump.  Late afternoon Sunday when the inflows were much lower, 1.45 MGD, plant operator switched the lead/lag order, as the pipe being used to feed the aeration tank is 14 inch in diameter, whereas it is normally 16 inches.  But due to ongoing plant upgrades, plant operations is relegated to using the smaller 14-inch line to aeration.   
Following the receipt of new information after the initial report on Monday 9/23, we learned from both a passerby and a Hull Police Officer, that the tank overflowed causing water to spillover and get beyond the treatment plant grounds to the cemetery access road and into the southeastern catch basin.  The Police Officer alerted Hull Dispatch, who contacted the treatment facility's 24-hour line, but no message was received.  Consequently, the plant staff were unaware of the situation until the following morning.  Upon discovering the overflow, staff collected samples from the catch basin and pumped out any standing water for disposal back at the plant as a precaution for the next possible rain event
The estimated overflow volume is now approximately 2,500 gallons.  This water either remained onsite, infiltrated the ground, or flowed into the catch basin, which discharges into the Hull Bay.  Any sewage debris was picked and powdered lime was spread liberally over the affected areas.

additionalInformation: A manhole on Moreland Avenue, at addresses #12 & 13, was discharging sewage due to the sewer line being surcharged from 4 inches of rain, from about 3 am 10am.   A full-size truck's front wheel was strategically parked to put significant pressure on the manhole cover to prevent any further discharge of sewage until the high flows lessened.   All solid debris was cleaned up immediately.

additionalInformation: The line break under the roadway in front of the home at 15 Eastman Avenue, Hull, MA, at the intersection of Pricilla Road.  A low-pressure sewer line coupling was found to be broken and leaking due to age and the sewage was flowing up and out through cracks in the road's asphalt. Sewage would only be emitted when one of four nearby homes, including #15 Eastman Avenue, discharged sewage from their house.  All four of the aforementioned houses discharging the sewage have in use at their houses "EOne" grinder pumps for their sewer concerns.  Local contractor EM Lofgrin was onsite at 9 am Saturday and soon commenced digging up the roadway to complete the repairs to the sewer line.  The overflowing sewage, less than 100 gallons, was contained to the roadway. Septage hauler Rosano-Davis was onsite as well Saturday morning and sucked up whatever accumulated sewage in puddles that they could with their pump truck.  Woodard & Curran staff put down liberal amounts of powdered lime about the spill areas and cleaned up any debris.
